Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 78
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Roofer
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Children Present: Being around children, Media / News: Related news, Known People: Related people
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Vignette:
Amir was seventy-eight years old, a roofer for more than four decades, and he had never thought much about the chemicals he worked with until that afternoon on a flat commercial roof in late July. A drum of industrial solvent had been left in the sun; the seal gave way as he hoisted it, and a hot, sweet-smelling liquid spilled across his arms and chest before he could drop the drum. The fumes hit his throat and eyes in a single burning wave. He coughed, rinsed his arms with a hose, and finished the job because that was what you did. He told no one. The memory of that moment—the shimmering heat, the chemical taste, the way his skin felt raw for days afterward—was something he could not pull up on purpose. When his wife asked years later what exactly had happened, he would say, “I don’t remember,” and that was true in the deliberate way: the sequence was gone, the faces of the other men on the roof fuzzy, the address of the building lost. But the feeling was not lost. At unpredictable moments, usually when he was alone in the garage or sitting on the porch after dinner, the same wave of nausea and dread would rise through his chest with no image attached, no story, just the full intensity of that July afternoon. He would grip the arms of his chair and wait for it to pass.

The consequences accumulated slowly. Amir had always been the grandfather who roughhoused with his grandchildren, who let them climb onto his lap without warning. After the exposure and the strange health scares that followed—a rash that took months to clear, a lingering cough, blood tests that his doctor called “nothing definitive”—he began to pull back. He told himself he did not want to expose the children to any residue, anything that might have soaked into his clothes or his skin years ago. But what frightened him most was not contamination. It was the touch itself. When a grandchild ran up and grabbed his arm from behind, his whole body would lurch; he would hear himself gasp, and the child would pull away, confused. He had come to believe that his body was no longer safe for others to touch, that any unexpected contact would reveal something damaged inside him. His wife noticed he stopped coming to family dinners. He said the noise bothered him, but the real reason was the children: their laughter, their sudden movements, their small hands.

Around the same time, he began avoiding the television in the living room. The local news ran a story about a chemical spill at a warehouse, and Amir’s stomach turned so violently that he had to sit down on the kitchen floor. After that, he changed the channel whenever a reporter used words like “toxin” or “exposure.” He also stopped going to the mosque on Friday, because a man from his old roofing crew sometimes sat in the back row, and the sight of that familiar face—the man who had stood next to him on the roof that day—sent a chill through him that took hours to fade. He told himself the man did not remember, that it was nothing, but his legs would not carry him past the door.

At home, Amir could not relax even in his own bedroom, which he knew was safe. He lay beside his wife with his eyes open, listening to the furnace hum, his muscles braced for nothing in particular. Sleep came in short, shallow pieces. He woke several times a night, his heart pounding, unable to say what had startled him. The startle had generalized: a hand on his shoulder in a grocery aisle, the weight of his wife’s hand on his back as she passed behind his chair—each time his body jerked before his mind could catch up. He had learned to keep a few inches of space between himself and anyone else, to sit with his back to the wall.

What brought him to the clinic was his wife’s quiet insistence after she found him crouched behind the couch, trembling, because the doorbell had rung and he could not explain why. He told the intake clinician that he was afraid of the memory he could not access, and he was even more afraid of what would happen if he ever did. He hoped, though he did not say it aloud, that someone could help him sleep without the feeling of the chemical heat on his skin. He was seventy-eight years old, and he was tired of not being able to remember the thing that would not let him go.
